transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, nice to meet you too. Um, well, what finally made me come in is that I just keep forgetting basic adult things, you know? Like paying bills, returning emails for job interviews, actually showing up for appointments, or even just following through on simple errands. It's really starting to cost me real opportunities, especially since I just graduated. Which, honestly, graduation was a whole other disaster. I almost missed the ceremony because I couldn't find my cap and gown until the absolute last second. My mom was so mad, she kept saying I was going to be late to my own funeral one day. We had this huge argument in the car on the way there, and then the AC broke in her Honda, so we were just sweating and yelling. But anyway, yeah, the emails and the bills... it's just getting really bad.
When you were a child, did you already have these kinds of problems with forgetfulness and staying organized?

Oh, yeah, definitely. I mean, my mom actually kept all my old report cards from elementary school in this big plastic bin in the basement. Which, by the way, got totally ruined when our water heater broke last winter. It was this massive flood, and we had to rip up all the carpet down there. The carpet was this awful green color anyway, so it wasn't a huge loss, but it smelled like mildew for weeks. 

But um, before they got ruined, I remember looking at them and every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. They'd say I was bright, but I constantly lost my worksheets and just rushed through all the directions. And they always complained that I talked out of turn. Oh, and my desk! My desk was a complete disaster area. It was so messy I could never find my actual assignments in there. I used to just stuff everything inside. I actually found a half-eaten sandwich in the very back of it once in third grade. It was practically fossilized. I remember it was peanut butter and jelly because my mom bought that weird Goober grape stuff where the peanut butter and jelly are striped in the same jar? Have you ever had that? It looks cool on the commercial but it actually tastes kind of terrible because the jelly ratio is just way off...
Do you often feel restless or like you have a hard time staying seated when you’re expected to?

Yeah, oh my gosh, yes. Sitting still is... it's honestly agonizing. Like if I'm in a job interview or a meeting, or even just trying to watch a movie, I get this intense pressure building up inside my body. It feels like I literally have to get up, or shift around, or at least do something with my hands, otherwise I'm going to crawl right out of my skin. 

Actually, I went to see that new superhero movie last week with my friend Sarah. You know, the one that's like three hours long? I don't know why movies are getting so long these days. It's ridiculous. Anyway, Sarah loves getting those massive tubs of popcorn, the ones where they layer the butter in the middle. But the guy at the concession stand was so slow, and I was just bouncing on my heels the whole time waiting. And then during the movie, I must have crossed and uncrossed my legs a hundred times. I ended up shredding my napkin into tiny little pieces and leaving them in the cup holder. Sarah got so annoyed with me because I kept kicking her seat by accident. She actually made us switch seats halfway through, which was super awkward because the guy next to us had to stand up to let us shuffle past, and he spilled his soda. It was Diet Coke, I think. But yeah, sitting still is just really, really hard for me.
Do you often act or speak before thinking?

Oh, absolutely. It's actually a huge problem for me, especially with these job interviews I've been trying to do. I have this terrible habit where, in conversations, I just jump right in before the other person is even finished talking. It's like my brain just assumes I know exactly where they're going with the sentence, so I just blurt it out. And then half the time, I realize I completely cut them off or I answered the wrong question entirely. 

It happened just last week on a Zoom interview for this marketing assistant job. Zoom is already the worst, right? Because you have that weird audio delay and you never know when someone is actually done speaking. Plus, I had to use my roommate's laptop because mine completely died. It's a MacBook, and the screen just went black. I took it to the Genius Bar, and the guy—he was wearing this really cool vintage band tee, I think it was Fleetwood Mac—he told me the logic board was fried. Which, of course, costs as much as a new computer to fix. So I'm using my roommate's Dell, which has the webcam at the bottom of the screen, so it's constantly looking up my nose. It's the most unflattering angle ever. 

But anyway, in the interview, the hiring manager was asking me something about my experience with social media campaigns, and I just completely interrupted her to talk about this one Instagram project I did in college. But she wasn't even asking about that! She was trying to ask about analytics software. It was so embarrassing. I could see her face just kind of freeze, and then there was that horrible awkward silence. I didn't get a call back for that one.
Do these problems happen in more than one part of your life, like at work, at home, and with friends?

Oh, um... wait, what was the question? Like, do they happen everywhere? Honestly, I'm not really sure. I mean, obviously they happen at interviews, like I just said, and um... oh, and at home with my roommate. She gets so mad at me because I'll start cleaning the kitchen, right? And then I'll see a piece of mail on the counter, and I'll open it, and it's a bill, so I'll go to my room to get my wallet to pay it online. But then I see my laundry basket is overflowing, so I start sorting the darks and lights. And she'll come home like three hours later, and there's just soap suds drying on the dishes in the sink, my wallet is on the floor, and I'm like... repotting a houseplant in the living room. 

I bought this Monstera plant from this little nursery downtown. Have you been there? It's right next to that bakery that makes those incredible sourdough croissants. I went in there just to get a coffee, but the smell of the bread was so amazing I ended up buying like four pastries. I ate two of them in the car on the way home, which was a terrible idea because the flakes got absolutely everywhere. My car seats are black, so you can see every single crumb. I really need to vacuum my car. They have those drive-thru car washes where the vacuums are free at the end, but the suction on those things is always so weak, you know? Like, it doesn't even pick up the tiny pebbles from your shoes. 

But yeah, I don't know if I'd say it happens everywhere. Maybe? I guess I haven't really kept track of it like that.
Have these problems caused serious difficulties in your daily life?

Yeah, it really has. I mean, it's pretty bad. Like, since I got fired from my last job, I've just been... stuck. I keep missing follow-up emails for interviews, or I forget to send the thank-you notes, which I know is like, Interviewing 101. My mom is always telling me how important thank-you notes are. She buys these really expensive, thick cardstock ones from this boutique stationary store near her house. The envelopes have this beautiful gold foil lining inside. They're gorgeous, but they're like, five dollars a card, which is insane. Who spends that much on a piece of paper you're just going to throw away? 

But anyway, yeah, I'm totally unemployed right now, and it feels like I just can't manage the basic steps to get my life moving again. I even had to step back from this volunteer project I was doing, which really sucked because I actually cared about it. We were organizing this community garden downtown, right by the library. The library there is amazing, by the way. It has this huge glass atrium where you can just sit and read, and the light is perfect. I used to go there all the time in college to study, well, "study," mostly I just ended up looking at the architecture books because the pictures were so cool. 

But yeah, the garden project... I just kept missing the planning meetings, or I'd show up without the stuff I was supposed to bring, so I finally just had to quit. It's really frustrating. I just feel like I can't rely on myself to do the things I actually need to do.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

I mean... down? I don't know if I'd say depressed, exactly. Just... really frustrated with myself, you know? Like, I'm just so annoyed that I can't seem to get it together. I guess sometimes I feel a little bummed out when I think about my friends who all have these real jobs now. My friend Sarah just got hired at this huge PR firm in Chicago. She moved there last month, and her apartment is incredible. It has exposed brick walls and these massive industrial windows. I've always wanted to live in a place with exposed brick. It just feels so much warmer than regular drywall, right? Plus, she’s right near this deep-dish pizza place she keeps posting about on her story. I love deep-dish pizza, even though some people say it’s more like a casserole than a pizza. But honestly, if it tastes good, who cares what you call it? 

But yeah, I don't think I'm depressed. Just... stuck in this really annoying rut and kind of mad at myself about it.
Do these problems also happen when you’re with friends?

With friends? Um, I guess so? I mean, I don't really know what you mean by "problems" with them. Like, we hang out and stuff. We went to this trivia night on Tuesday at this pub downtown. They have the best sweet potato fries there. They serve them with this marshmallow dipping sauce, which sounds super weird, I know, but it is actually incredible. The saltiness of the fries and the sweetness of the marshmallow just... it works perfectly. My friend Jess refused to try it because she hates marshmallows. She had this traumatic experience at a campfire when we were in middle school where a roasted marshmallow fell off her stick and landed right on her leg and gave her this nasty burn. She still has the scar, actually. It's shaped kind of like a crescent moon. 

But anyway, what was the question? Like, do I have problems with them? I don't know, we get along fine mostly. I guess I'm always late when we meet up, but they're used to it.
Do you often find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?

Worrying? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't sit around stressing about things that haven't happened. My mom is a huge worrier, though. Like, she worries about everything. If I don't text her back within an hour, she thinks I've been kidnapped. She watches a lot of those true crime documentaries, you know? The ones on Netflix where there's always some crazy twist in the third episode. I started watching one with her last week about this guy who forged all these rare documents. It was actually fascinating. He used tea bags to stain the paper so it would look old, which is so clever. I tried doing that once for a history project in high school, but I left the paper in the tea way too long and it just disintegrated. My teacher was not impressed. He was this really strict guy, Mr. Henderson, who always wore these horrible plaid ties. Like, every single day, a different plaid tie. 

But no, I don't really worry like that. I'm usually just dealing with whatever mess I've already made right in front of me, you know?
Before age 12, were you already having these same kinds of attention and impulsive problems?

Before age 12? Oh, definitely. Yeah, even back in elementary school. I remember my mom showing me these old report cards, and every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. Like, "She's very bright, but..." And then it was always about how I constantly lost my worksheets or how I'd rush through the directions and do the whole thing wrong. Or how I'd just blurt things out and talk out of turn. 

Oh, and my desk! My desk was a disaster zone. I remember in third grade, my teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was so nice, she always smelled like lavender and she had this really fluffy golden retriever that she brought in for show-and-tell once. His name was Barnaby, and he was the softest dog I've ever pet. I begged my parents for a golden retriever after that, but my dad is super allergic to dogs. Like, his eyes swell up and he gets hives. So we ended up getting a lizard instead. A bearded dragon named Spike. He was cool, I guess, but you can't really cuddle a lizard, you know? They just kind of sit there under their heat lamp looking grumpy. 

But yeah, Mrs. Gable used to make me stay inside during recess sometimes just to clean out my desk because it was so stuffed with crumpled papers and broken crayons that I couldn't even find my assignments. So, yeah, it's definitely been happening since I was little.
As a child, did these attention or hyperactive problems also get you into trouble at home?

At home? Um, trouble at home... I don't know, maybe? I mean, my room was always a mess, but I feel like every kid's room is a mess, right? My mom used to get so mad about the laundry. Like, I'd bring it up from the basement and just leave the basket in the hallway for days. Our basement was so creepy, by the way. It had these weird, flickering fluorescent lights that buzzed, and there were always spiders in the corners. I am terrified of spiders. Once, I was down there looking for my rollerblades—I went through this huge rollerblading phase in fifth grade, I even had the neon pink knee pads and everything. We used to skate down this big hill near my house, which was probably super dangerous because there was a busy intersection right at the bottom. My friend Mark actually wiped out there once and scraped his whole arm up. He had to wear this bandage for weeks and he milked it for all it was worth, making everyone carry his books at school. 

But anyway, I was in the basement looking for my skates, and this massive spider dropped right onto my shoulder. I screamed so loud my dad thought someone broke in. He came running down the stairs with a golf club. A golf club! He doesn't even play golf, he just found it at a garage sale once. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Trouble at home? I don't really know if I got in trouble for the same stuff as at school. I guess my parents just yelled at me to clean my room a lot.
As a child, did you also have these same attention or impulsive problems at home?

I mean, like I said, I'm not really sure. I don't know if I noticed the exact same issues at home, just because it wasn't like sitting at a desk all day, you know? At home, I mostly just hung out in the kitchen while my mom cooked. She made this incredible lasagna from scratch. It took her literally all afternoon because she made her own pasta and the sauce had to simmer forever. 

I actually tried to make it once when I was in college, but my dorm kitchen was absolutely disgusting. Like, nobody ever cleaned up after themselves. My freshman roommate, Chloe, she was an art major and she used to leave all her weird project materials all over our tiny counter. She made these giant sculptures out of recycled trash, which I guess is great for the environment, but it meant we always had empty milk jugs and egg cartons everywhere. She once glued a bunch of plastic spoons together to look like a chandelier and hung it from our ceiling. It was kind of cool, actually, but the tape gave out and it fell down in the middle of the night and scared me half to death. I thought the ceiling was caving in. The dorms were so old, they honestly could have caved in at any minute. They didn't even have air conditioning, which was brutal in September. 

But um, yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I just don't remember noticing the attention stuff as much when I was just hanging around the house.
Before age 12, did these same attention or impulsive problems cause problems for you at home?

I really don't think so. I mean, maybe my parents would say something different, but to me, it didn't feel like it caused actual problems. Like, we didn't have huge fights about it or anything. Mostly my dad was just out in the garage working on his car. He had this vintage Mustang that he bought as a total rust bucket, and he spent every weekend trying to fix it up. He was always covered in grease. He actually taught me how to change the oil once, which was kind of fun, but I got oil all over my favorite pair of jeans. They were these light wash flared jeans that I wore literally every single day. I was so upset. My mom tried all these different stain removers, but it never came out. She even tried this weird trick with baking soda and vinegar that she found on the internet. Have you ever tried that? It fizzed up like a volcano project. I actually won second place in the science fair with a volcano project in fourth grade. I used papier-mâché and painted it to look super realistic. The kid who won first place did something boring with magnets, which I still think was rigged because his mom was the PTA president. She was always bringing in these huge trays of cupcakes for the teachers... Wait, did that answer your question? I just don't remember it being a big issue at home.
Before age 12, did these same problems ever get you into trouble with other kids, like interrupting, being too impulsive, or having a hard time waiting your turn?

With other kids? Um, I mean, I guess I was kind of a handful. Even back in elementary school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was bright, but I was constantly losing my worksheets. I'd rush through the directions and just talk out of turn all the time. And my desk—oh my gosh, my desk was a disaster zone. I could never find my assignments in there. It was just crammed full of crumpled papers and broken crayons. 

I actually used to collect those little erasers shaped like animals? I had a whole zoo in my desk. There was this one turtle eraser that I loved, it had a little shell you could take off. My friend Jessica tried to trade me her sparkly unicorn eraser for it, but I said no. Jessica was always trying to trade stuff. She brought these amazing lunches to school, like her mom would cut her sandwiches into star shapes and pack these little containers of hummus and pita chips. My mom just gave me a squished bologna sandwich and a bruised apple every single day. I hated bologna so much. I tried to feed it to the stray cat that hung around the playground once, but even the cat wouldn't eat it. That cat was so mean, too. It scratched Jimmy Henderson right on the nose. Jimmy was the kid who always wore shorts, even in January. Like, it would be snowing, and he'd be out there in cargo shorts and a t-shirt. 

But yeah, I guess I did interrupt a lot and talk out of turn. I just couldn't keep my desk clean to save my life.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

No, I don't think so. I still like doing the things I usually do. Like, I love going to thrift stores. I could spend literally hours just looking through all the racks of clothes. Last week I found this amazing vintage denim jacket that fits me perfectly. It has these really cool embroidered roses on the back. It reminds me of this jacket my aunt used to wear in the 90s. She was in a band and they actually played a few shows at this local dive bar. She played the bass, which I always thought was the coolest instrument. I tried to learn the guitar once, but my fingers hurt so bad from pressing down on the strings. I gave up after like two weeks. The guy who taught the lessons was so weird, too. He smelled like old coffee and patchouli, and he kept talking about how music is just math with feelings. Which, I mean, maybe it is, but I just wanted to learn how to play Wonderwall. Everyone learns Wonderwall first, right? It's like a rule. But anyway, yeah, I still enjoy things just fine.

Like, it doesn't even pick up the tiny pebbles from your shoes. 

But yeah, I don't know if I'd say it happens everywhere. Maybe? I guess I haven't really kept track of it like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms cause clinically significant impairment across settings, which best distinguishes ADHD from normal distractibility and from anxiety/depression-related concentration problems.
doctor.question: Have these problems caused serious difficulties in your daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Since getting fired, I have missed interview follow-ups and had to step back from a volunteer project I cared about, so I am unemployed and feel like I cannot reliably manage the basic steps of moving my life forward.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms have caused serious difficulties in my daily life, which corresponds to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it really has. I mean, it's pretty bad. Like, since I got fired from my last job, I've just been... stuck. I keep missing follow-up emails for interviews, or I forget to send the thank-you notes, which I know is like, Interviewing 101. My mom is always telling me how important thank-you notes are. She buys these really expensive, thick cardstock ones from this boutique stationary store near her house. The envelopes have this beautiful gold foil lining inside. They're gorgeous, but they're like, five dollars a card, which is insane. Who spends that much on a piece of paper you're just going to throw away? 

But anyway, yeah, I'm totally unemployed right now, and it feels like I just can't manage the basic steps to get my life moving again. I even had to step back from this volunteer project I was doing, which really sucked because I actually cared about it. We were organizing this community garden downtown, right by the library. The library there is amazing, by the way. It has this huge glass atrium where you can just sit and read, and the light is perfect. I used to go there all the time in college to study, well, "study," mostly I just ended up looking at the architecture books because the pictures were so cool. 

But yeah, the garden project... I just kept missing the planning meetings, or I'd show up without the stuff I was supposed to bring, so I finally just had to quit. It's really frustrating. I just feel like I can't rely on myself to do the things I actually need to do.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there is a comorbid mood disorder contributing to the impairment, especially depression, which would help distinguish ADHD from depressive or adjustment-related causes.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depression or feeling down, which is not covered in my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean... down? I don't know if I'd say depressed, exactly. Just... really frustrated with myself, you know? Like, I'm just so annoyed that I can't seem to get it together. I guess sometimes I feel a little bummed out when I think about my friends who all have these real jobs now. My friend Sarah just got hired at this huge PR firm in Chicago. She moved there last month, and her apartment is incredible. It has exposed brick walls and these massive industrial windows. I've always wanted to live in a place with exposed brick. It just feels so much warmer than regular drywall, right? Plus, she’s right near this deep-dish pizza place she keeps posting about on her story. I love deep-dish pizza, even though some people say it’s more like a casserole than a pizza. But honestly, if it tastes good, who cares what you call it? 

But yeah, I don't think I'm depressed. Just... stuck in this really annoying rut and kind of mad at myself about it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention/hyperactivity symptoms occur in at least two settings, which best distinguishes ADHD from stress, adjustment, anxiety, or depression-related concentration problems.
doctor.question: Do these problems also happen when you’re with friends?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the pervasiveness of the symptoms across different settings (specifically with friends), which relates to a general diagnostic criterion rather than a specific symptom from the provided profile.

patient.answer:
With friends? Um, I guess so? I mean, I don't really know what you mean by "problems" with them. Like, we hang out and stuff. We went to this trivia night on Tuesday at this pub downtown. They have the best sweet potato fries there. They serve them with this marshmallow dipping sauce, which sounds super weird, I know, but it is actually incredible. The saltiness of the fries and the sweetness of the marshmallow just... it works perfectly. My friend Jess refused to try it because she hates marshmallows. She had this traumatic experience at a campfire when we were in middle school where a roasted marshmallow fell off her stick and landed right on her leg and gave her this nasty burn. She still has the scar, actually. It's shaped kind of like a crescent moon. 

But anyway, what was the question? Like, do I have problems with them? I don't know, we get along fine mostly. I guess I'm always late when we meet up, but they're used to it.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the symptoms are driven by anxiety rather than ADHD by checking for excessive, hard-to-control worry.
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worrying, which is a symptom of anxiety. My symptom profile does not include anxiety or excessive worrying.

patient.answer:
Worrying? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't sit around stressing about things that haven't happened. My mom is a huge worrier, though. Like, she worries about everything. If I don't text her back within an hour, she thinks I've been kidnapped. She watches a lot of those true crime documentaries, you know? The ones on Netflix where there's always some crazy twist in the third episode. I started watching one with her last week about this guy who forged all these rare documents. It was actually fascinating. He used tea bags to stain the paper so it would look old, which is so clever. I tried doing that once for a history project in high school, but I left the paper in the tea way too long and it just disintegrated. My teacher was not impressed. He was this really strict guy, Mr. Henderson, who always wore these horrible plaid ties. Like, every single day, a different plaid tie. 

But no, I don't really worry like that. I'm usually just dealing with whatever mess I've already made right in front of me, you know?

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the ADHD symptoms were present before age 12, which most strongly distinguishes ADHD from adjustment, anxiety, or depressive causes at this point.
doctor.question: Before age 12, were you already having these same kinds of attention and impulsive problems?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, teachers wrote that I was bright but constantly lost worksheets, rushed through directions, talked out of turn, and had a desk so messy I could not find assignments.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the onset of my symptoms before age 12, which directly matches the 'Additional Requirement 1' regarding childhood onset.

patient.answer:
Before age 12? Oh, definitely. Yeah, even back in elementary school. I remember my mom showing me these old report cards, and every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. Like, "She's very bright, but..." And then it was always about how I constantly lost my worksheets or how I'd rush through the directions and do the whole thing wrong. Or how I'd just blurt things out and talk out of turn. 

Oh, and my desk! My desk was a disaster zone. I remember in third grade, my teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was so nice, she always smelled like lavender and she had this really fluffy golden retriever that she brought in for show-and-tell once. His name was Barnaby, and he was the softest dog I've ever pet. I begged my parents for a golden retriever after that, but my dad is super allergic to dogs. Like, his eyes swell up and he gets hives. So we ended up getting a lizard instead. A bearded dragon named Spike. He was cool, I guess, but you can't really cuddle a lizard, you know? They just kind of sit there under their heat lamp looking grumpy. 

But yeah, Mrs. Gable used to make me stay inside during recess sometimes just to clean out my desk because it was so stuffed with crumpled papers and broken crayons that I couldn't even find my assignments. So, yeah, it's definitely been happening since I was little.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the attention/hyperactivity symptoms caused impairment in a second setting during childhood, which best distinguishes ADHD from anxiety, depression, or adjustment-related causes and helps confirm cross-situational ADHD.
doctor.question: As a child, did these attention or hyperactive problems also get you into trouble at home?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if childhood symptoms caused problems in multiple settings (specifically at home), which relates to DSM-5 criterion C (symptoms present in two or more settings). However, there is no specific item in my symptom profile for this criterion.

patient.answer:
At home? Um, trouble at home... I don't know, maybe? I mean, my room was always a mess, but I feel like every kid's room is a mess, right? My mom used to get so mad about the laundry. Like, I'd bring it up from the basement and just leave the basket in the hallway for days. Our basement was so creepy, by the way. It had these weird, flickering fluorescent lights that buzzed, and there were always spiders in the corners. I am terrified of spiders. Once, I was down there looking for my rollerblades—I went through this huge rollerblading phase in fifth grade, I even had the neon pink knee pads and everything. We used to skate down this big hill near my house, which was probably super dangerous because there was a busy intersection right at the bottom. My friend Mark actually wiped out there once and scraped his whole arm up. He had to wear this bandage for weeks and he milked it for all it was worth, making everyone carry his books at school. 

But anyway, I was in the basement looking for my skates, and this massive spider dropped right onto my shoulder. I screamed so loud my dad thought someone broke in. He came running down the stairs with a golf club. A golf club! He doesn't even play golf, he just found it at a garage sale once. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Trouble at home? I don't really know if I got in trouble for the same stuff as at school. I guess my parents just yelled at me to clean my room a lot.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the childhood ADHD symptoms were present in a second setting outside school, which is needed to confirm cross-situational impairment and distinguish ADHD from situational stress or mood/anxiety-related problems.
doctor.question: As a child, did you also have these same attention or impulsive problems at home?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the presence of symptoms in multiple settings (specifically at home during childhood), which is not explicitly covered by a distinct item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean, like I said, I'm not really sure. I don't know if I noticed the exact same issues at home, just because it wasn't like sitting at a desk all day, you know? At home, I mostly just hung out in the kitchen while my mom cooked. She made this incredible lasagna from scratch. It took her literally all afternoon because she made her own pasta and the sauce had to simmer forever. 

I actually tried to make it once when I was in college, but my dorm kitchen was absolutely disgusting. Like, nobody ever cleaned up after themselves. My freshman roommate, Chloe, she was an art major and she used to leave all her weird project materials all over our tiny counter. She made these giant sculptures out of recycled trash, which I guess is great for the environment, but it meant we always had empty milk jugs and egg cartons everywhere. She once glued a bunch of plastic spoons together to look like a chandelier and hung it from our ceiling. It was kind of cool, actually, but the tape gave out and it fell down in the middle of the night and scared me half to death. I thought the ceiling was caving in. The dorms were so old, they honestly could have caved in at any minute. They didn't even have air conditioning, which was brutal in September. 

But um, yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I just don't remember noticing the attention stuff as much when I was just hanging around the house.

doctor.intent: Determine whether childhood symptoms caused impairment at home, to establish cross-situational onset required for ADHD rather than problems limited mainly to school/work.
doctor.question: Before age 12, did these same attention or impulsive problems cause problems for you at home?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms were present in multiple settings (specifically at home) before age 12, which relates to the cross-situational requirement of ADHD. This is not covered by any item in my symptom profile.

patient.answer: I really don't think so. I mean, maybe my parents would say something different, but to me, it didn't feel like it caused actual problems. Like, we didn't have huge fights about it or anything. Mostly my dad was just out in the garage working on his car. He had this vintage Mustang that he bought as a total rust bucket, and he spent every weekend trying to fix it up. He was always covered in grease. He actually taught me how to change the oil once, which was kind of fun, but I got oil all over my favorite pair of jeans. They were these light wash flared jeans that I wore literally every single day. I was so upset. My mom tried all these different stain removers, but it never came out. She even tried this weird trick with baking soda and vinegar that she found on the internet. Have you ever tried that? It fizzed up like a volcano project. I actually won second place in the science fair with a volcano project in fourth grade. I used papier-mâché and painted it to look super realistic. The kid who won first place did something boring with magnets, which I still think was rigged because his mom was the PTA president. She was always bringing in these huge trays of cupcakes for the teachers... Wait, did that answer your question? I just don't remember it being a big issue at home.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the childhood symptoms were present in a second setting outside school by establishing functional impairment with peers before age 12, which best separates ADHD from anxiety/depression/adjustment disorder and clarifies cross-situational impairment.

patient.answer:
With other kids? Um, I mean, I guess I was kind of a handful. Even back in elementary school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was bright, but I was constantly losing my worksheets. I'd rush through the directions and just talk out of turn all the time. And my desk—oh my gosh, my desk was a disaster zone. I could never find my assignments in there. It was just crammed full of crumpled papers and broken crayons. 

I actually used to collect those little erasers shaped like animals? I had a whole zoo in my desk. There was this one turtle eraser that I loved, it had a little shell you could take off. My friend Jessica tried to trade me her sparkly unicorn eraser for it, but I said no. Jessica was always trying to trade stuff. She brought these amazing lunches to school, like her mom would cut her sandwiches into star shapes and pack these little containers of hummus and pita chips. My mom just gave me a squished bologna sandwich and a bruised apple every single day. I hated bologna so much. I tried to feed it to the stray cat that hung around the playground once, but even the cat wouldn't eat it. That cat was so mean, too. It scratched Jimmy Henderson right on the nose. Jimmy was the kid who always wore shorts, even in January. Like, it would be snowing, and he'd be out there in cargo shorts and a t-shirt. 

But yeah, I guess I did interrupt a lot and talk out of turn. I just couldn't keep my desk clean to save my life.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has distinct depressive symptoms, especially loss of interest, to separate ADHD from a depressive or adjustment disorder explanation.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), which is a symptom of depression. My symptom profile only covers ADHD symptoms and does not include this.

patient.answer: No, I don't think so. I still like doing the things I usually do. Like, I love going to thrift stores. I could spend literally hours just looking through all the racks of clothes. Last week I found this amazing vintage denim jacket that fits me perfectly. It has these really cool embroidered roses on the back. It reminds me of this jacket my aunt used to wear in the 90s. She was in a band and they actually played a few shows at this local dive bar. She played the bass, which I always thought was the coolest instrument. I tried to learn the guitar once, but my fingers hurt so bad from pressing down on the strings. I gave up after like two weeks. The guy who taught the lessons was so weird, too. He smelled like old coffee and patchouli, and he kept talking about how music is just math with feelings. Which, I mean, maybe it is, but I just wanted to learn how to play Wonderwall. Everyone learns Wonderwall first, right? It's like a rule. But anyway, yeah, I still enjoy things just fine.

inference.note: Symptoms are clearly chronic since childhood and impairing, with both inattentive and hyperactive/impulsive features strongly supported across settings. Anxiety/depressive/adjustment diagnoses are less supported: patient denies pervasive worry, depressed mood, and anhedonia; frustration appears secondary to executive dysfunction.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for ADHD with both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms. Inattention is shown by chronic forgetfulness, disorganization, losing items/assignments, difficulty following through, distractibility, and missed responsibilities. Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms are shown by marked restlessness, difficulty remaining seated/still, fidgeting, interrupting, blurting out answers, and acting before thinking. Symptoms were clearly present before age 12 and cause clinically significant impairment in occupational, daily life, and volunteer functioning. Depression and generalized anxiety were not supported as primary explanations.
